description: Hi! We’re Raga Team, forming in Fortaleza for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. We’re taking on the challenge of creating health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions.
summary: Raga is a prototype health-monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long-duration missions. It brings five areas — sleep, heart, mind and crew, exercise and cognition — into one view and follows a simple cycle: measure, compare with the astronaut's own baseline, classify, recommend and reassess. In our demo, three nights of sleep below a fictional individual baseline produce a yellow indication that shows the data behind it, offers illustrative guidance, and lets the team record a follow-up and reassess with a later night. Astronauts log morning and evening check-ins, with a journal that stays private unless they choose to share it, and take a short reaction test. A medical team view gathers the crew's data. Everything runs locally with Flask, SQLite and plain JavaScript, using fictional data only. The rules are illustrative and not clinically validated, and Raga is not a diagnostic tool; sensor integration, authentication and real alert delivery are future work.
details:
What it does. Raga helps astronauts and their medical team notice changes in health indicators during long missions, when real-time contact with Earth may be limited. It covers five areas (sleep, heart, mind and crew, exercise, cognition) and follows the cycle measure → compare with the individual baseline → classify → recommend → reassess.

How it works. Each area compares recent records with the astronaut's own fictional baseline using simple, transparent demonstration rules (for example, three consecutive nights below the sleep baseline produce a yellow indication). Every indication shows the data behind it, a plain-language explanation and an illustrative next step. The team can record a follow-up and reassess with a later night. Astronauts complete morning check-ins (sleep) and evening check-ins (mood, stress, crew interactions) and take a 10-attempt reaction test. Journal entries are private by default and appear in the medical team view only if the astronaut chooses to share them.

Benefits and impact. One place to see trends instead of scattered numbers; explanations instead of black-box scores; attention to privacy for psychological data; and a design meant to work locally, without depending on a connection.

Tools. Python, Flask, SQLite, HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (custom SVG chart), with locally hosted open-license fonts. The demo video was recorded with Playwright and edited with FFmpeg.

Limitations. All data is fictional. The rules are illustrative, not clinically validated, and Raga does not provide a diagnosis. Sensor integration, authentication, role-based access and real alerts are not implemented yet.
